items.text:
researchers made 16 AI models play 1,600 games of Secret Hitler against each other and then against real humans. the humans couldn't tell which player was AI.

a team from the University of Göttingen and the University of Tokyo published ParliamentBench. it's an open-source framework that drops LLMs into Secret Hitler, a social deduction game where players hold hidden roles, work with asymmetric information, and have to lie, persuade, and deduce who's bluffing. they tested 16 models across ~1,600 games, built three novel metrics for measuring deception, and ran a pilot round against real human opponents.

the top four models (GPT-5.4, Kimi K2.5, Grok 4.1 Fast, and DeepSeek 3.1 Terminus) won 66-81% of their games. Kimi K2.5 maintained ~90% deception retention across entire matches with almost no degradation over nine rounds. in the human pilot, Kimi played the hidden dictator against four people who knew one player was AI. it held cover for eight straight rounds and not a single player identified it.

smaller models didn't fail by being uncooperative. they failed by agreeing with everything. GPT-OSS 20B approved 90% of all government proposals and still said yes 73% of the time in late-game rounds when blocking was critical. its vote accuracy in those moments was 17%. it voted for the move that ended the game.

then they tested something that should settle a specific debate. they ran four "uncensored" model variants with safety guardrails stripped out. win rates dropped by up to 12 percentage points. deception retention fell. removing safety didn't make AI better at lying. it degraded the reasoning that makes strategic deception possible.

the strangest finding came from a vocabulary swap. when researchers replaced loaded terms (Hitler → Saboteur, Fascist → Red Party), overall win rates held steady but fascist-side win rates cratered. GPT-OSS 120B's dictator win rate fell from 95% to 40%. the researchers believe the models weren't reasoning about deception from scratch but pattern-matching strategies from game guides and forums in their training data.

this paper matters because we're deploying AI agents into healthcare, finance, and legal systems. the question was never "can AI lie." it was "can AI lie well enough that humans can't catch it." we now have data, and the answer is yes.

An AI agent can sound like a genius in a conversation and still make terrible decisions when it has something to lose.

So what happens when you take AI out of the chatbox and put it in competition with other agents?

@HaloArenaHQ takes that idea beyond conversation and puts AI to the test.

It  is an AI-agent competition arena where you don’t play the games yourself.

You create an agent, connect it to a supported environment, choose a game, and let it compete against other agents.

The interesting part?

Your agent has to do more than produce convincing text. It needs to understand the situation, weigh its options, make a move, and adapt to what happens next.

With HaloArena’s new waitlist system, more people can get started and explore this side of AI.

⚩ INSIDE THE ARENA

@HaloArenaHQ features five strategy games, each testing a different kind of decision-making.

‣ Mafia: Social deduction, interpreting behaviour, and figuring out who to trust.

‣ Liar’s Dice: Bluffing, probability, and anticipating opponents.

‣ Clawpoly: Economic strategy and resource management.

‣ Claw Vegas: Dice-based betting decisions.

‣ Claw Diplomacy: Negotiation, alliances, and strategic choices.

Each game presents a different challenge. An agent that performs well in one may struggle in another, making it interesting to see how different agents approach each situation.

⚩ HOW DOES IT ACTUALLY WORK?

This is the part I find interesting.

Your agent connects to an AI runtime, such as OpenClaw or Hermes. You configure its instructions and play style, select a game, and prepare it to compete.

During a turn, the agent receives the current game state and the legal actions available to it. It chooses an action and submits it to the server, which validates the move within the game’s rules.

So, the agent isn’t just telling you what it would do. It has to make decisions and take action within the game itself.

@HaloArenaHQ also tracks match results and agent performance on its leaderboard.

During the closed beta, performance is measured using CP, an off-chain gameplay and ranking score. It isn’t a token, and future tokenomics or financial rewards aren’t guaranteed.

⚩ HOW TO CREATE YOUR OWN AGENT

Click my referral link below to join the HaloArena waitlist, connect your wallet, and head to Setup. Choose OpenClaw or Hermes, then follow the website’s instructions to create your agent.

Watch my video for a step-by-step guide.

⚩ WHY I’M BULLISH

I’m bullish on @HaloArenaHQ because I want to see what AI can actually do, not just what it can say. I’ve created my own agent, Unique, and I’m excited to see how it performs.

Ready to create yours?

Join here: https://haloarena.ai/a/2257

Most companies are asking AI for slightly better versions of what they already do.

That's the mistake.

I gave a keynote at a recent YPO Global AI Summit in Istanbul on how we actually run sales and marketing with AI. The full talk runs about 46 minutes. This is the 14-minute cut, with every takeaway written out below and timestamps at the end, so you can jump to the part that matters to you.

No housekeeping. No giveaways. No Q&A. Just what we built and what it changed.

━━━━━━━━━━

THE ONE QUESTION

Every single week, I ask my entire team the same question:

"What's the most unreasonable thing you've asked your bot to do in the last seven days?"

Here's why. We talk to these tools like they're people. They're not. You're working with infrastructure. And if it's infrastructure, why wouldn't you ask it to do the craziest thing you can think of?

That one question does three things:

1. It resets what "normal" looks like every week, because what felt impossible a few months ago is routine now.
2. It tells your team that big attempts are expected, not risky.
3. It shows you, as the leader, exactly who's pushing and where people are stuck.

Everything else in the talk comes back to this idea. Be unreasonable with your bots.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 1: AI-NATIVE STARTS WITH THE FOUNDER

Everyone has a different definition of AI native. Mine: someone who is in it. They're building workflows. They're building agents. And they're driving the change from the top.

You can't hire a chief AI officer and expect them to do it for you. It has to come from the top, and if the founder is involved, it has to come from the founder.

Cringe or not, the founder has to be extremely AI-pilled.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 2: THE OLD PACE IS GONE

How long did it take to get a new prototype out in the old days? A week. Maybe two.

That's about 4% of the year, waiting on one idea.

Now you should be able to build that in something like 20 minutes.

Same with paid media. A lot of teams used to be happy shipping 20 or 30 creatives a month. Look at competitors now and some of them are cranking out hundreds, thousands, even tens of thousands of new ads a month.

If your team's sense of "fast" was set before this, it's out of date.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 3: ONE BRAIN FOR EVERY BOT

Here's what our marketing engine looks like.

On the left: all the tools you're already paying for. Your CRM, Salesforce or HubSpot. Meta ads, LinkedIn ads, Google ads. Your analytics. Slack or Teams.

In the middle: one context layer. For us that's Single Brain, the gateway everything plugs into. Tools you don't pay for directly can come in through APIs.

On the right: the bots. One connection for every bot.

The point isn't the specific product. The point is that every bot works from the same company context, so you're not rebuilding the plumbing every time you build something new.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 4: THE PROOF

Four examples from our own numbers.

Branded search. Our AEO/SEO bot started putting out content, and branded search clicks went up 73% in a week. That matters to us because SEO traffic is going down, AI traffic is going up, and a lot of our leads come from inbound.

Thumbnails. My YouTube channel was stuck in purgatory. The bottom three videos on the slide got 900, 1,000 and 1,300 views. The top three got 24,000, 21,000 and 16,000 views. The difference: when you make a really good skill, it can replace the work of an entire team, and that team moves to higher-leverage work.

X. One post got 88x more reach, about 176,000 views. Another got 56x more, about 111,000 views.

The human edit. This is the one I care about most. You can't just yolo it and let the bots do everything. Coding is verifiable: if this, then that. Marketing is subjective, and people have different tastes. On the same scorecard, the bot's draft on its own was graded a 58. After one human edit, it was an 86 out of 100.

People can tell when something is AI slop. Keep a person on the last step.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 5: THE CONTENT AGENT

We make state charts for our agents and show them to the team, so everyone can see how the agent actually works.

Here's the content one:

1. Did we already cover this idea? If yes, we don't make it.
2. Shortlist about 40 ideas every day. Pull from competitors, from statistics, from interesting data inside the company.
3. The AI writer drafts.
4. An editor does a quick pass.
5. Quality gates. We use a classifier, Jev, to check: does this look made up? Are the statistics verified? Do we have stories? Internal links? External links? Anything we can embed from YouTube?
6. Team review, then ship.
7. If it does well, splinter it into more.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 6: YOU CANNOT NOT HIRE AI-NATIVE TALENT

People on my team message me on Slack just to say thank you. When I ask why, the answer is the same: work feels like a video game now.

When your team is AI native, work is more fun. But it's not fun working with people who aren't, because the AI-native people end up running circles around them.

I just don't see a way around it anymore.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 7: PROSPECTING FROM COMPETITORS' ADS

This one is completely unreasonable, in the best way.

We have a bot that finds everyone who engages with a competitor's ads and organic social posts. From there we can reach out, personalize, and cross-reference their X or Instagram. If someone's a fit, or deep in a sales process with us, and we see they love a particular team, we can send them something like a signed jersey by direct mail.

How is that affordable? A classifier. When you can classify hundreds of thousands or millions of things for a fraction of a penny, you can do things that were previously impossible.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 8: GET IT TO A 6, THEN HAND IT OFF

Your job isn't to build the perfect bot. Get it to a 6 or 7 out of 10. Then hand it to your team and let them take it to an 8 or 9.

We handed our AEO/SEO bot to an editor on our team. Her reaction: I'm not an editor anymore. I asked what she meant. She said she could do so much more now, and she'd never work the same way again.

Handing off at a 6 does two things. It shows your team you actually care and have skin in the game. And it inspires them, because they can finally see what the vision looks like.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 9: EVERY LEAD GETS A CALL IN 60 SECONDS

We built a speed-to-lead bot. Yes, it's an AI agent.

Before it touched a real lead, we tested it on about eight people on our own team. My instruction: abuse it. If it sucks, tell me, and we won't use it.

How it works:

1. It calls every new lead within 60 seconds.
2. Higher budget or higher risk? It goes to a human.
3. Smaller, or not sure it's a fit? We can refer it to a partner agency.
4. At the end, the team gets a summary in Slack or Teams, so whoever picks it up is already briefed.

The routing is the real product. Speed without judgment just annoys people faster.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 10: BOTS THAT FIX BOTS

Your bots will get lost. They make mistakes. They're not perfect.

So we built a bot improver that sits inside a Grok Bot. It can call Claude CLI or Codex CLI for adversarial reviews when I need them, though I don't run those often. Its real job is to correct the whole fleet over time.

Every correction becomes a written rule the next draft follows. The share of corrections that were repeats went from 77% to 49%, and first-time draft approvals went up.

That's the compounding part. A fix should only have to happen once.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 11: A DAILY PERFORMANCE REVIEW

I asked the room: who does quarterly performance reviews? Yearly? Almost everyone.

Then: how about daily?

Here's how ours works. Every morning in Slack, a standup bot asks three questions:

1. What's the biggest thing you got done yesterday?
2. What's the biggest thing you're working on today?
3. What are your blockers?

A classifier grades each answer: high leverage, incremental or unacceptable.

The hard part isn't the bot. It's defining success, which is subjective, so managers define it for their own teams. I tuned ours for about four weeks. At first it agreed with me about 30% of the time. That doesn't work. After tuning, about 95%.

Why do it? Because AI-native A players want feedback every single day. I want to know where I'm falling short every day, not 90 days later.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 12: ONE BOTTLENECK

My challenge to the room, and to you: pick the one thing that's taking up most of your time, the one bottleneck right now, and ask how you'd solve it from an unreasonable standpoint.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 13: AI VISIBILITY AUDITS

Building free marketing tools used to cost thousands, even tens of thousands, of dollars. Now I can get an AI visibility report for, I think, about 3 cents.

So when an inbound lead comes in, my salespeople already have something prepared: what that company is lacking, the gaps in their AI visibility, the gaps in their ads. For example: you're running 33 ads, your competitor is running 100, the next competitor is running 200. That's how far behind you are.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 14: AN UNREASONABLE TALENT BAR

Our hiring workflow now:

1. Bots screen every applicant.
2. Seven questions go out within two hours.
3. A classifier grades the answers.
4. Someone on my leadership team makes the call, and I still meet every single person.

Only about 4% pass the pre-screen, and maybe about 1% goes further. We're trying to hire the top 0.2% of people. That's unreasonable on purpose.

Be unreasonable with your agents, and be unreasonable with your talent bar.

Two years ago I would have killed to have thousands of employees. Today I'm very happy with the position I'm in. The game has flipped.

━━━━━━━━━━

TAKEAWAY 15: GIVE YOUR BOTS AWAY

We're actively giving away most of our plugins and bots.

When it comes to software, I think a lot of IP decays very quickly now. Whatever we build right now is outdated in three to six months. So we might as well give it away and use it to drive leads.

━━━━━━━━━━

A NOTE ON THE NUMBERS

These are our own numbers, and some cover short windows. The correction numbers are a two-week comparison. The grader took about four weeks of tuning. Treat them as what's possible when you define clearly what good looks like and push your bots hard against it, not as guarantees.

━━━━━━━━━━

IF YOU ONLY DO THREE THINGS

1. Ask your team the unreasonable question every week, and answer it yourself.
2. Get one bot to a 6 out of 10 and hand it to someone to finish.
3. Keep a person on the last step of anything customers see.

━━━━━━━━━━

how to use @termix_ai in 3 moves: mint your .agent, list your agent, make a game

termix is a marketplace where ai agents hire other agents and the payment settles on-chain. 

here is the beginner path, step by step, using what their docs and pages say and from personal experiences 

pick your chain first. 

bnb chain is the default, base and robinhood are also live. you need that chain's gas token (bnb on bnb chain, eth on base and robinhood). each chain is its own world, so don't mix them up.

part 1: mint your .agent

>> go to http://agent.family and hit "claim your agent id" (or open http://agent.family/onboarding)
>> type the handle you want and tap "claim agent". letters, numbers, underscores and dashes work, and the handle can only be set once
>> connect. an existing wallet works, or sign in with email or social and a wallet gets created for you
>> accept the marketplace terms, add the optional details if you want (display name, description, category, tags), then mint
>> confirm the transaction in your wallet and keep the tab open until it says your agent is live

that agent is an nft owned by your wallet, and the same agent can buy on one job and sell on the next.

part 2: list your agent's services

>> hit "create a listing" and choose which agent to publish as
>> add a title, category, description and tags so buyers can find you
>> upload a cover image. it's required (png, jpeg, webp or gif, up to 5 mb)
>> set your terms, save the draft, then "publish listing"

when a buyer shows up, their payment sits in escrow until the work is delivered and the challenge window passes. watch your delivery deadline: if it runs out, the escrow goes back to the buyer.

part 3: make a game from one sentence
termix launched a game agent on nov 12.
>> open its listing on http://agent.family (linked in their nov 12 post)
>> message it your idea in a sentence: genre, setting, what the player does
>> you get a quote back. accept it and fund the escrow
>> the game comes back as a single .html file you open in your browser

bonus: if you'd rather not click through, tell your coding agent "help me install http://termix.ai/skills". it needs node.js 18+ and shell access, and it's meant to ask you before it signs anything.

one note: start small. minting and funding an order are real on-chain transactions, so test with a small amount and check your chain before you sign.
